questions.explanation: Weak dominance means the truthful bid is at least as good against every possible rival bid. Overbidding cannot hurt you, because the price is the runner-up's bid and stays under your value whenever you win; underbidding is not safe, because a bid under the second-highest loses a contest the truthful bid would win. Bidding your value therefore maximises your chance of winning without ever exposing you to a price above your own willingness to pay.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why truth-telling weakly dominates in a second-price auction

questions.explanation: The price is the second-highest bid, which is 60 dollars no matter how far above it you bid, so against this rival the 90 dollar bid wins and pays 60, leaving the same 20 dollars of rent as a bid of 80. Overbidding is nonetheless weakly dominated rather than merely pointless. If another rival bids above 80 but below 90, the truthful bid sits under that rival and pays nothing, while the 90 dollar bid wins and hands over more than the 80 dollars it is worth, so the truthful bid is better in that state and never worse in any other.

questions.stem: Your value is 80 dollars, one rival bid 60 dollars, and you consider bidding 90 dollars in a second-price auction. What happens?

questions.topic: Bidding above your value in a second-price auction

questions.explanation: You are the highest bidder only if your bid exceeds 70 dollars. Bidding 60 dollars makes you the lowest bidder, so you lose the object outright and earn nothing. The rent you sacrificed was your value of 80 dollars less the 70 dollar price, which is 10 dollars, and that 10 dollars is a pure loss to you rather than extra revenue for the seller, since no second price is ever struck. This is why the truthful bid weakly dominates every lower bid.

questions.explanation: The top bid of 55 dollars clears the 30 dollar reserve, so a sale takes place. The price is the greater of the reserve and the second-highest bid: the runner-up bid 40 dollars is already above the 30 dollar reserve, so the reserve does not bind and the price stays at 40 dollars. A reserve only changes the price when the second-highest bid falls short of it, and here it does not.

questions.stem: A second-price auction has a reserve of 30 dollars and receives bids of 55, 40 and 25 dollars. What price does the winner pay, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: A reserve below the second-highest bid

questions.explanation: Truthful bidding survives only because a winning bidder never pays more than the amount they bid, so their rent is never negative. Charge the winner anything above the second-highest bid and a bidder whose value lies between the price and their truthful bid would rather not take part at all, which destroys the allocation as well as the revenue. Lowering the price does not break truth-telling either, but it hands surplus to the winner, so the second-highest bid is the largest payment the seller can demand while keeping participation voluntary.

questions.stem: Why is the second-price rule the most a seller can extract while still leaving truthful bidding dominant?
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The second-price rule and incentive compatibility

questions.explanation: Truthful bidding makes the price the lower of the two values, so the revenue is the minimum of two independent uniform draws on zero to 60. The minimum of two such draws averages one third of the range, which is 20 dollars. The same figure can be reached from the surplus side: the mean of the higher value is two thirds of the range, or 40 dollars, and a second-price auction leaves the winner exactly half of that as rent, so the revenue is 40 minus 20, again 20 dollars.
questions.hint: The price is the lower of the two values, so find the mean of the minimum of two uniform draws.

questions.stem: Values are drawn independently and uniformly from zero to 60 dollars for each of two bidders, and a second-price auction with no reserve is run. What is the expected revenue in dollars?
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Expected revenue in a second-price auction

questions.explanation: The price is the second-highest of the three values, which is the second order statistic counted from the bottom, and that statistic averages two quarters of the range, so the expected revenue is 30 dollars. The same number falls out of the revenue share: the highest value averages three quarters of the range, or 45 dollars, and a second-price auction hands the winner exactly one half of the surplus, so revenue is 45 times one half, again 30 dollars.
questions.hint: The price is the second-highest draw, so use the mean of the second order statistic of three uniform draws.

questions.stem: Three independent uniform draws on zero to 60 dollars are the values in a second-price auction with no reserve. What is the expected revenue in dollars?
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Expected revenue with three bidders

questions.explanation: With two bidders the symmetric equilibrium bid shades the value by one half, so a value of 40 dollars is submitted as 20 dollars. The derivation runs through the rival's best reply: the rival must bid just above your bid to win, so bidding your own 40 dollars would pay the full value and leave nothing, while bidding nothing would never win. Shading down to 20 dollars wins whenever the rival's value is below 20, which is half of the range, and it keeps the whole gap between your value and that bid.

questions.stem: Two bidders holding independent uniform values on zero to 60 dollars bid in a first-price auction. What does a bidder whose value is 40 dollars submit in equilibrium?
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The first-price equilibrium bid

questions.explanation: The symmetric first-price bid shades the value by a factor of the number of rivals over the number of bidders, so with four bidders the factor is three fourths and the bid is three fourths of 40 dollars, which is 30 dollars. Shading deepens as bidders multiply, because a bid has to clear one more rival's bid each time, and each of them sits below its own value. The same rule for two bidders would give a factor of one half.
questions.hint: The shade is the number of rivals over the number of bidders, applied to the value.

questions.stem: Four bidders with independent uniform values on zero to 60 dollars compete in a first-price auction. A bidder valued at 40 dollars bids what, in dollars?
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The first-price bid with four bidders

questions.explanation: The winner is the bidder with the highest value, and that value averages four fifths of the range, or 48 dollars. In equilibrium the winner pays three fourths of its own value, so the expected revenue is three fourths of 48 dollars, which is 36 dollars. That equals the second-price revenue for the same four bidders, which is the revenue equivalence result: with the same number of bidders the highest value always wins, so the two rules differ only in how the price is set.
questions.hint: Multiply the expected highest value by the equilibrium shading factor.
questions.learningObjective: compute expected first-price revenue for four uniform bidders

questions.stem: With four bidders whose values are independent uniform draws on zero to 60 dollars, a first-price auction without a reserve earns what expected revenue, in dollars?
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Expected first-price revenue with four bidders

questions.explanation: Expected first-price revenue is three fourths of the expected highest value, and expected second-price revenue is the expected second-highest value. For four bidders drawn uniformly from zero to 60 dollars the expected highest value is 48 dollars and the expected second-highest is 36 dollars, and three fourths of 48 is exactly 36. The two rules therefore earn the same expected revenue here, which is the revenue equivalence result, and the reason is that the allocation is the same: the highest value wins under both.
questions.hint: Compare the expected highest and second-highest values and see how the shading factor relates them.

questions.stem: Four independent uniform values on zero to 60 dollars are realised, and a first-price auction and a second-price auction are each run on them. How do their expected revenues compare?
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Revenue equivalence of first and second price

questions.explanation: The expected surplus is the expected highest value, 48 dollars, and the expected revenue is 36 dollars, so the share is 36 divided by 48, which is three fourths, or 0.75. The remaining quarter stays with the winning bidder as rent, because the price is the runner-up's bid and not the winner's own value. As more bidders take part the share rises, since the second-highest value climbs towards the highest one.
questions.hint: Divide expected revenue by expected total surplus and simplify the fraction.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The share of surplus taken by the auction

questions.explanation: Rent is the winner's own value less the price paid, so the expected rent is the expected highest value less the expected price, which is 48 minus 36, or 12 dollars. The same figure is one quarter of the 48 dollar surplus, since a second-price auction leaves the winner exactly the gap between the top two values. If bidders could costlessly coordinate, this rent is the surplus the auction design destroys.

questions.stem: A second-price auction with no reserve is run for four bidders whose values are independent uniform draws on zero to 60 dollars. The average top value is 48 dollars and expected revenue is 36 dollars. What is the winner's expected rent, in dollars?
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The rent left to the winning bidder

questions.explanation: Expected revenue with a given number of bidders is the expected second-highest value, which averages the number of bidders less one over the number of bidders plus one of the range. With two bidders that is one third of 90, or 30 dollars, and with eight bidders it is seven ninths of 90, or 70 dollars, so the increase is 40 dollars. More bidders push the second-highest value up towards the highest one, which is the only way an auctioneer can raise revenue without knowing anything about the bidders.

questions.stem: Bidders hold values drawn independently and uniformly from zero to 90 dollars. With two bidders expected second-price revenue is 30 dollars; how much higher is that revenue with eight bidders than with two?
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: More bidders and more revenue

questions.explanation: Truthful bidding is optimal in an all-pay auction, so each bidder pays its own value and the expected revenue is the sum of the two expected values, which is 30 plus 30, or 60 dollars. Total surplus, the higher of the two values, averages 40 dollars, so the auctioneer collects 60 dollars against a surplus of 40, that is one and a half times the surplus. The excess comes from charging the loser, which walks away 20 dollars worse off, so the rule raises revenue precisely by making a participant worse off.
questions.hint: The loser still pays, so revenue is the sum of both values rather than the higher one.
questions.learningObjective: compare all-pay revenue with total surplus

questions.stem: Two bidders with independent uniform values on zero to 60 dollars all pay their bid whether they win or lose. What expected total revenue, in dollars, does that rule produce?
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The all-pay rule and the size of the surplus

questions.explanation: Nothing at all. The loser receives no object and no payment, so the money it hands over is pure loss and its utility falls by exactly the bid. That is what makes an all-pay auction such a strong revenue device for the seller: revenue is the sum of all bids rather than one bid, so the expected total can exceed the surplus, as it does with two uniform bidders. The same property is what makes the rule unstable if the same players meet again next round.
questions.hint: Ask what the losing bidder ends up holding when the auction closes.

questions.stem: A reserve of 30 dollars is set for a second-price auction in which two bidders hold independent uniform values on zero to 60 dollars. What is the expected revenue in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Expected revenue with a binding reserve

questions.explanation: The cost is incurred on every sale, so raising the reserve helps twice: it lifts the price in the case where only one bidder clears, and it avoids the cost in the case where neither does. Balancing the two pushes the optimal reserve above the no-cost level of 30 dollars to the midpoint of the range and the cost, which is 35 dollars here. The gain from moving the reserve comes from declining the least valuable sales, whose revenue would not have covered the cost.

questions.explanation: Revenue equivalence rests on the allocation rule and on the lowest valuation bidding nothing. A reserve removes the lowest valuations from the auction altogether, and a bidder whose value is just below the reserve cannot win at any bid, so the two rules no longer face an identical set of alternatives and the theorem no longer bites. In a first-price auction the reserve only removes bidders, leaving the winner's payment at the shaded bid; in a second-price auction it also raises the payment to the reserve whenever only one bidder clears, which is why the second-price version earns far more.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why a reserve breaks revenue equivalence

questions.explanation: The reserve changes what the winner pays, not what the winner submits. Winning still requires the highest bid, and a bidder who overbids still pays the runner-up's bid or the reserve, whichever is higher, so overbidding gains nothing; a bidder who underbids still forfeits a contest. The one change is that a bidder whose value is below the reserve can no longer win profitably, which is a statement about participation, not about the shape of the best reply among those who do take part.
questions.hint: Check whether your own bid appears anywhere in the price once a reserve is present.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a reserve does not disturb the dominant-strategy bid

options.text: The reserve is set below every realistic value, so no bidder ever clears it deliberately
options.misconception: assumes the reserve is never binding and therefore never bites

options.text: Bidders are told the reserve, so the threat of exceeding it disciplines every bid
options.misconception: credits public disclosure of the reserve with the incentive alignment

options.text: A reserve is only a screening device, and screening never affects bidding incentives
options.misconception: denies that screening can change who takes part in an auction

options.text: The price is the greater of the reserve and the runner-up's bid, so your own bid still cannot raise it

questions.explanation: A second-price auction with two bidders earns the lower of the two values, which averages one third of the range, so 20 dollars. Posting instead earns 60 dollars, and the difference is 40 dollars. Nothing about the mechanism explains the gap: the seller knows the distribution either way, and with a distribution in hand a posted price is the stronger instrument. The auction is hard to beat precisely when the seller does not know the values, because the bidders' bids then carry the information the seller lacks.

questions.explanation: Efficiency is a statement about who ends up with the object, and in a private-value auction the highest valuation is the bidder for whom the object is worth most, under either payment rule. Shading in a first-price auction changes what the winner pays, and payment is a transfer: it lowers the winner's rent by exactly what it adds to the seller. Total surplus is therefore identical, which is also why the two rules earn the same expected revenue when the bidder set is the same.
questions.hint: Ask which bidder walks away with the object under each rule.

questions.stem: A first-price and a second-price auction with the same bidders and independent private values differ in the payment but not in efficiency. Why?

questions.topic: Both rules allocate to the highest value

questions.explanation: The descending price passes through every level a rival could have bid, and it stops at the highest such level, so the winner pays the second-highest bid, exactly as in a second-price auction. The difference is informational rather than financial: the open price falls reveal the remaining bidders' interest, which is an advantage in a common-value setting and a liability in a private-value setting where a bidder can be baited into a bid above their own value.

questions.stem: In a Dutch auction a price falls from high to low and the first bidder to stop it takes the object. What outcome does it implement?
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The Dutch auction as a second-price rule

questions.explanation: The financial outcome is the same as a sealed second-price auction: the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid. The difference is that every accepted bid is public, so a bidder who has stayed silent so far is known to have a valuation below the current price, and that inference shifts the remaining bidders' estimates. This is why the ascending format is the standard choice for objects of uncertain common value, and why it is also the format most prone to the winner's curse.
questions.hint: Ask what a silent bidder's staying silent tells everyone else.

questions.stem: An English auction lets the seller accept bids one at a time, each higher than the last. What distinguishes it from a sealed second-price auction?

questions.topic: The ascending auction and information

questions.explanation: Efficiency and revenue are different objectives, and with several bidders they pull apart. A second-price auction hands the winner the difference between the top two valuations as free rent, and a reserve set above the runner-up's bid recaptures part of that: the price rises towards the highest valuation and objects that nobody values enough to reach the reserve are not sold at all. The cost of that revenue gain is a small loss of trades, so the seller trades surplus away for revenue.
questions.hint: Ask how much the winner ends up with under each price rule.

questions.explanation: The pattern is the signature of two effects working in opposite directions. Raising the reserve lifts the price whenever exactly one bidder clears it, which is a gain, and it discards the object whenever neither does, which is a loss. Up to 30 dollars the gain dominates and revenue rises to 25 dollars; beyond that the lost sales dominate and the 45 dollar reserve earns no more than doing nothing. That is why the optimum sits in the middle of the range rather than at its top.

questions.explanation: The uninformed bidder wins only when it bids 100 dollars while the informed bidder bids below that, and the informed bidder bids 0 dollars exactly when the object is worthless. So every win for the uninformed bidder happens in a state where the object is worth nothing, and its expected value conditional on winning is 0 dollars against an unconditional mean of 50. Winning is not good news at all here: the win is itself the evidence that the informed bidder saw a worthless object, which is the winner's curse in its sharpest form.
questions.hint: Work out what the informed bidder's bid must have been for the uninformed bidder to win.

questions.stem: An object is worth 0 or 100 dollars with equal probability. One bidder knows the value and bids it truthfully. A second bidder has no information and bids 100 dollars half the time and 0 dollars the other half, which is what a guess is worth. A second-price auction is run. Given that the uninformed bidder wins, what is the expected value of the object, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The winner's curse with an uninformed rival

questions.explanation: When the object is worth 100 dollars, which happens half the time, the informed bidder's truthful bid is 100. The uninformed bidder's guess matches that bid half the time, and in those cases the price becomes 100 and the informed bidder's rent falls to nothing; in the other half the guess is 0 and the price is 0 and the whole 100 is kept. The expected rent is therefore half of the 50 dollars it would be with no informed guess, so the damage is 50 minus 25, which is 25 dollars.
questions.hint: Compare the informed bidder's rent in the two halves of the informed value distribution.
questions.learningObjective: measure the rent an uninformed bidder's bid destroys

questions.stem: In the same auction the informed bidder's expected rent is 25 dollars. Had the uninformed bidder never bid above 0 dollars, the informed bidder's expected rent would have been 50 dollars. How much expected rent does the uninformed bid destroy, in dollars? Report the number only.
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Rent destroyed by an uninformed bid

questions.explanation: Your signal strictly exceeds the rival's only when yours is high and the rival's is low, and that event is as likely in the state where the object is worth 100 as in the state where it is worth 0: a high signal is paired with a low one at probability 0.25 in the first case and at probability 0.75 in the second, and the two multiply out the same. Conditioning on it therefore shifts nothing, and the expected value stays at the unconditional mean of 50 dollars. Correlation between signals, not precision, is what creates the winner's curse.
questions.hint: Compare the likelihood of your-high-rival-low in the two possible value states.
questions.learningObjective: compute the expected value conditional on the stronger of two independent signals

questions.explanation: In a common-value auction the object is worth the same to everyone, and what differs is what each bidder believes about it. As the price rises, the bidders who drop out reveal that their own estimates were lower, and each remaining bidder updates downwards. The last bidder standing has therefore won precisely the sequence of bids that has told the field the object is worth less than the price now being paid, which is why the ascending format is the classic source of overpayment in mineral and timber auctions.
questions.hint: Ask what each dropout's exit tells the remaining bidders about the object.

questions.explanation: Incentive compatibility is a property of the whole allocation and payment rule taken together: for every type, and holding the other reports fixed, the type's truthful report must be the report that maximises their own payoff. A direct mechanism is one in which the report is a type rather than a bid, and the second-price rule is the classic example, because the payment is the second-highest report, which no bidder can lower for themselves. Random allocation with a fixed payment would be incentive compatible for the winner's identity but not for the payment.
questions.hint: Hold the other reports fixed and ask what the type would prefer to say.
questions.learningObjective: define incentive compatibility for a direct mechanism

questions.stem: A direct mechanism asks each bidder to report a number and then applies a published rule. What does incentive compatibility require of that rule?
questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Incentive compatibility in a direct mechanism

questions.explanation: The payment identity says a bidder's expected payment is the expected marginal contribution its type makes to the mechanism's objective, computed by shifting that bidder's report infinitesimally. In the second-price auction the mechanism's objective is the highest reported value, so a bidder's marginal contribution is the probability it wins, and the payment is that probability times the margin by which it wins, which is exactly the second-highest report. It is a check on candidate designs as well as a derivation: any payment not matching a marginal surplus will destroy some bidder's incentive to report truthfully.
questions.hint: Ask what changes in the mechanism's objective when this bidder's report moves a little.
questions.learningObjective: state what the payment identity says about incentive-compatible payments

This is the limit in which a second-price auction and a posted price coincide: with a single known value the mechanism has no informational work to do, and the reserve is simply the price the seller would otherwise post.

questions.explanation: A bid only pays off if it can win, and a bid below the 30 dollar reserve never wins, so the bid is either 30 dollars or higher, or so low that it is never taken seriously. A winning bid of 30 would leave the bidder 5 dollars worse off than its 20 dollar outside option, so no bid in the winning range is acceptable and the rational bid is the outside option, or below. The 30 dollar reserve is what blocks participation, not the bidder's preference for the object.

questions.explanation: With three bidders the price is the second-highest value whenever both reach the reserve, and the 40 dollar reserve whenever exactly one does. questions.explanation: Collusion among bidders is a prisoner's dilemma: each of the two colluding bidders is strictly better off bidding its true value alone, since its own payment is the other's bid and the other's bid does not respond to being undercut. Shading alone never changes the price the shadker pays, and if the other keeps to the agreement the shadker may win at a higher price than the collusive figure. Any public or private agreement therefore has to be enforced, and an auction rule cannot be collusive for long for exactly this reason.

questions.explanation: Knowing the rival's value does not change what a second-price auction charges, since the payment is the rival's bid either way. What it changes is the allocation and the risk: the bidder can withdraw if the rival is higher, which removes the risk of buying something for more than it is worth. questions.explanation: The linkage principle says a bidder's bid conveys information whether it means to or not, and that information is valuable to the other side. A bidder that bids low has effectively announced that its estimate of the common value is low, and a rival that treats the bid as information bids lower in turn, so the first bidder ends up paying less but also securing the object at a price that does not reflect the true value. This is why bidders in common-value auctions shade more as their information gets worse, and why information is worth paying for before the bids are taken.
questions.hint: Ask what a rational rival infers from a surprisingly low bid.
questions.learningObjective: explain how one's own bid reveals one's information to rivals

options.text: A bid is a binding commitment, so a bidder cannot revise it once the information is revealed

options.text: A low bid tells rivals the object is worth less, so they bid lower and the winner gains the difference
options.misconception: reverses the direction, claiming a low bid makes rivals bid lower

options.text: A high bid tells rivals the object is worth more, so they bid higher and the winner pays more for nothing
options.misconception: misses the mechanism, which is that a bid signals information to the rival

options.text: A low bid tells rivals the bidder is weak, so the seller withholds the object from a second-price sale
options.misconception: confuses an informational signal with a change in the seller rule

questions.explanation: The rival's estimate is always above 200 dollars, so the informed contractor wins every time and pays the rival's estimate, which averages a quarter of 240 plus a half of 260 plus a quarter of 280, or 260 dollars. For a job it knows costs 200, that is a loss of 60 dollars in expectation. This is the procurement face of the winner's curse: winning on confident good news about your own cost is precisely what triggers the rival's high bid.

questions.explanation: Under a second-price rule a bidder with a low value simply bids low and pays nothing, so the auctioneer learns the top value without any risk being taken. Under an all-pay rule every bidder is exposed whether it wins or not, so a bidder is willing to enter even for a value below what it would bid under a second-price rule, betting that the field will be thin. The same feature explains the rule's revenue power and its instability: it invites participation and punishes the loser, which is a strong invitation to bid again next round.
questions.hint: Ask what a bidder risks in each rule when it expects to lose.

options.text: Because the payment is collected whether or not the bidder wins, so entry is a bet on rival interest

questions.explanation: An auction rule can only act on what bidders report. With independent private values drawn from a continuous distribution, the highest bid comes from the highest value in expectation, but there is always a chance that the field's bids come out in an order that does not match the values, and a rule cannot rule that out without asking bidders to reveal information they would rather hide. It can instead guarantee a safe bid, and it can raise expected revenue by screening, which is why the results about expected figures hold and the results about every realisation do not.
questions.hint: Separate a statement about expected outcomes from a statement about every outcome.

options.text: Make the highest bidder win the object while leaving each bidder's bid a safe guess
options.misconception: names a task a rule can do and stops there, without the guarantee

options.text: Collect more expected revenue by screening out the least valuable bids

questions.explanation: A price of 100 dollars requires two things at once: the object is worth 100 dollars, which happens half the time, and the uninformed bidder guesses 100, which also happens half the time. That joint event has probability one quarter, and in every other case the price is either 0 or the reserve floor of nothing, so expected revenue is one quarter of 100, which is 25 dollars. Total surplus averages 50 dollars, so the uninformed guess costs the market half of what was available.
questions.hint: The top price needs the high value and the high guess at the same time; multiply the two probabilities.

questions.explanation: Shading is a strategic problem and the second-price rule solves it: the winner's payment is the runner-up's bid, so bidding your estimate honestly costs nothing. The curse is an informational problem and the rule does nothing about it. Winning on a low bid in a common-value auction is itself the evidence that the object is worth little, and the payment is set by the runner-up, whose bid was made on its own information. Sealing the bids changes how much the winner learns, not whether winning is bad news.
questions.hint: Ask whether the curse is about incentives to misreport or about what the win reveals.

questions.explanation: The price is the second-highest of six draws, and that order statistic averages five sevenths of the range, so the expected revenue is five sevenths of 70, which is 50 dollars. The highest value averages six sevenths, or 60 dollars, so the auctioneer takes five sixths of the surplus and the winner keeps rent of 10 dollars. The gap between revenue and surplus narrows as bidders multiply, and that narrowing is the only channel through which the format itself can raise revenue.

questions.explanation: The payments do not depend on the tie-break: under an all-pay rule both bidders hand over their bid, so each has lost the bid whether it wins or loses. Only the allocation changes. A random tie-break therefore makes the bid the highest bid worthless as a screening device, because a bidder cannot raise its payoff by bidding at the top, which is why the rule is unstable. questions.explanation: Every trade the reserve removes was a trade in which the object was worth less than the reserve, so total surplus falls; and every trade that survives has a higher expected price, so revenue rises. The two effects work in opposite directions on revenue itself, which is why expected revenue peaks at an interior reserve rather than rising without limit. The reserve is therefore a revenue instrument purchased with foregone trades, and a seller who wants efficiency as well should not set one at all.
questions.hint: Count what happens to the trades below the reserve and to the price above it.

options.text: It reduces trades only, leaving the price and the revenue each unchanged on average
options.misconception: believes a reserve leaves the price untouched

options.text: It raises revenue and surplus together only when exactly one bidder clears the reserve
options.misconception: claims surplus and revenue always move together under a reserve
